sources.headline: Deadly fire at Canada military base moved a kilometre 'in 30 to 60 seconds'
sources.text: The fire that killed four members of the Canadian military and injured dozens of others on Saturday spread with alarming speed, accounts suggest.It broke out in a grassy training area at a base in the province of Alberta and spread rapidly due to strong winds."The fire was 1km (0.6 miles) away when the wind shifted," said Maj-Gen Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division of the Canadian Armed Forces. "It is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 30 to 60 seconds."Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime". Officials have ruled out the possibility of "any terrorist activity".Speaking in the House of Commons on Monday, Carney said the fire was "driven by ferocious winds". "The fire jumped nearly a kilometer less than a minute to where the soldiers were gathered," he said, adding that the cause of the fire was not yet known.Carney said the injuries occurred "in the space of a few minutes".The blaze began at about 16:00 (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases. The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died.Of the 39 injured people receiving care in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told Canadian broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright.Tributes are being paid to the servicemen who died. Patricia Farrell, the mother of Shaun Farrell, wrote on Facebook that it was "with heavy hearts that we share the news that our son, Shaun Farrell, has passed away to be with our Heavenly Father".Wong received a tribute from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, of which he was part. The regiment was "deeply saddened", it wrote in a Facebook post of its own. It sent "heartfelt condolences to [the group's] families, friends, and fellow soldiers".The mother of Goulding, Sonia Monk, said her late son was an exceptional athlete and a natural leader. "He was always the guy who kept everybody's spirits up," she told CBC. "He really was the light of my life."Canadian PM Carney said on Monday that Goulding was known as "a generous and deeply loyal friend". Lykkemark, Carney said, "was known for his gift for lightening a hard day, his quick wit - he dreamed of a career in law enforcement". "These were sons, brothers, partners, friends, young men with bright futures who chose to serve our country and who died in that cause," Carney said. In recounting Saturday's events, Rutland told reporters that members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range.He told reporters that officials knew about the fire on the base for several hours, but it was decided that training "could carry on for a certain amount of time"."I spoke to my commander last night, and he said within 30 seconds to a minute they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them," Rutland said.Rutland said it was not yet known what exactly caused the fire.Some witnesses had said they had heard explosions, fuelling speculation that oil and gas infrastructure may have been hit and sparked the fire. But Rutland said authorities "do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure".The Canadian Armed Forces has said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity". Forecasters had issued a wind warning on Saturday for large parts of Alberta, predicting wind gusts of up to 90km/h (66mph), Canadian broadcaster CBS said.According to Rutland, the investigation may take at least a month.Wainwright, about 130 miles east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries. About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day.

sources.headline: Four people killed in ‘violent, fast-moving’ fire at Canadian military base
sources.text: Four people have been killed and dozens more seriously injured after a “violent, fast-moving” fire tore through one of Canada’s busiest military training bases in Alberta, the country’s prime minister said on Sunday.Mark Carney called the incident “one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime”.Winds up to 96km/h (60mph) fed the blaze, which broke out at 4pm on Saturday during high-intensity combat training at the base. Alberta premier Danielle Smith said at a press conference on Sunday evening that 39 people were in hospital after the fire, with at least 19 of them in a critical condition.Maj Gen Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division, said that a grass fire ignited in a training area of the military base, which spread quickly. The cause of the fire was being investigated, he said.The military identified those killed as Sgt Morgan Wong of the Loyal Edmonton Regiment and Privates Shaun Farrell, Aidan Goulding and Hayden Lykkemark of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light infantry. All four were serving with the battalion, based in Edmonton.Rutland said military officials knew about the fire for hours but believed it was contained before winds suddenly shifted, sending flames racing toward the soldiers.“The fire was a kilometre away when the wind shifted. That is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 36 seconds,” he said at a news conference in Edmonton.“I’ve certainly never seen anything like it,” he added.The fire broke out during high-intensity combat training involving Charlie Company of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light infantry, sweeping into the area where the simulated attacks were taking place.About 84 soldiers were in the company, which was split between a grenade range and an area where soldiers practised attacks on simulated enemy positions.“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces whom we have lost. And I have asked the flags on all federal buildings to be flown at half-mast to honour them,” Carney told the nation in an address from Ottawa. “We are praying for the wounded.”Carney said he had requested a “detailed account” from military officials on the ground about what had happened.Emergency crews and military personnel gather at the Wainwright Health Centre on Saturday. Photograph: John Ulan/The Canadian Press/APThe country’s defence minister, David McGuinty, described the event as a “terrible incident” as he travelled to the scene to meet senior officials and first responders.“I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory,” he said, adding that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) were involved in the investigation.McGuinty did not provide details about what caused the incident and the Canadian armed forces said on Sunday that its “immediate priority” was notifying next of kin and helping those affected by the fire. The armed forces and federal, provincial and local authorities were coordinating the emergency response, they said.Canada’s top soldier, Gen Jennie Carignan, who serves as chief of the defence staff, called the incident “a profoundly difficult moment for the entire Canadian armed forces”.The nearby community of Wainwright was providing hospital and firefighting support. Photograph: Jennifer Gauthier/ReutersThe nearby community of Wainwright provided hospital and firefighting support. Flares were spotted in the sky and military medical paratroopers dropped in on a local school football field.Health staff in ‌Edmonton said a “code orange,” or mass-casualty ​event, was declared to coordinate ​the medical response for patients being transported from Wainwright.A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180km (112 miles) north-west of Wainwright, told Canada’s national broadcaster that Wainwright’s healthcare facilities had been inundated.“This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton,” Dr Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra hospital, told CBC News. “It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15- to 25-year disaster.”Officials asked people in Edmonton to avoid the emergency department at the University of Alberta hospital in order to prioritise victims from the military base. Air ambulances were dispatched from Saskatoon and Edmonton.Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, said the nation was ‘in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces whom we have lost’. Photograph: Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press/APThe fire at the military base swept into the area where the simulated attacks were taking place, crossing established firebreaks before being contained with help from municipal firefighters.The Canadian military said there were no indications of terrorism.On Sunday, the Alberta premier described the fire as “heartbreaking” and said it had affected many military personnel.“On behalf of the government of Alberta, I extend my deepest condolences to the families who have lost loved ones and wish those who have been injured a full recovery. Our thoughts are also with the military personnel, families and colleagues facing uncertainty and grief during this incredibly difficult time,” Smith said.The premier said many of the injured would require “weeks and months” of specialised, intensive medical care. She is due to travel to meet senior officials in Edmonton.The Saskatchewan premier, Scott Moe, said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.CFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military bases. Photograph: Daphne Lemelin/AFP/Getty ImagesCFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.“On behalf of the Nato military committee, we extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in the tragedy at CFB Wainwright, and our wishes for a full recovery to all the injured,” Adm Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, the chair of the Nato military committee, posted on social media. “Those who fell there served our common security, and the military committee will honour their memory.”Canada’s Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, said he had spoken with Carney and the defence minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.“Pray for Wainwright, everyone,” Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.

Four soldiers killed in Canada military base fire: Everything we know
Why you can trust Sky News

The four Canadian soldiers who died during a training exercise at the weekend did so when a grass fire spread "a kilometre in 36 seconds", officials said.

Military personnel said 39 people were in hospital after the fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright on Saturday.

Sergeant Morgan Wong, of the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, and Privates Shaun Farrell, Aidan Goulding and Hayden Lykkemark of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry were killed.

All four had been serving with the battalion, based in Edmonton.

Alberta premier Danielle Smith said 19 of the injured are in a critical condition, while many will require "weeks and months" of specialised, intensive medical care.

Fifty investigators are examining the fire at the military base, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Monday.

Military base fire - as it happened

Image:
Fire crews at the scene in Alberta. Pic: John Ulan/The Canadian Press/AP

"A fire was burning in the training area. Driven by ferocious winds, the fire jumped nearly a kilometre in less than a minute to where soldiers were gathered," Mr Carney said.

He added investigators had not determined what sparked the grass fire.

"We will get the answers to what caused this terrible tragedy, as expeditiously and transparently as necessary," Mr Carney later told reporters.

The King, who is monarch of Canada, said in a message of condolence that he and the Queen were "greatly shocked and saddened".

"Our deepest sympathy and heartfelt condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who have lost their lives, and with all those who have been injured or otherwise affected at this most difficult time," he wrote.

Mr Carney described the incident as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada's military on home soil.

Flags on federal buildings across the country will be lowered to honour the victims, he added.

Some 85 soldiers were carrying out "high intensity" combat training using live munitions when the grass fire started at around 4pm local time.

Major General Wade Rutland said military officials were aware of the blaze for hours and thought it was contained.

However, he said the area was experiencing high winds and gusts of up to 60mph at the time, sending flames racing toward the soldiers.

He added: "The fire was a kilometre away when the wind shifted. That is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 36 seconds.

"I've certainly never seen anything like it."

sources.headline: 4 dead, dozens injured after fire at Canadian military base, officials say
sources.text:
Updated on: October 19, 2026 / 8:56 AM EDT
/ CBS/AP
Add CBS News on Google
Four Canadian service members were killed and 39 people injured, including 19 critically, when a fast-moving fire overtook soldiers conducting live-fire combat training at a military base in Alberta, officials said Sunday.Prime Minister Mark Carney described the incident as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada's military on domestic soil. He ordered flags lowered to half-staff on federal buildings nationwide and said he'd requested a detailed account and formal briefing on the incident at Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Wainwright.Maj. Gen. Wade Rutland said military officials knew about the grass fire for hours but believed it was sufficiently contained to allow training to continue before winds suddenly shifted, sending flames racing toward the soldiers."The fire was a kilometer away when the wind shifted. That is not normal for a fire to move a kilometer in 36 seconds," he said at a news conference in Edmonton.Rutland said a commander at the scene told him soldiers went from seeing no fire to having flames upon them in less than a minute.Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said Sunday that injured patients were transferred from the base to four hospitals across Alberta. She said some suffered severe burns and could face weeks or months of intensive treatment. After the incident happened on Saturday, a doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 120 miles northwest of the military base, told Canada's national broadcaster that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city as health care facilities around the base became "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people needing care.
"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15- to 25-year disaster."
Emergency crews and military personnel gather at the Wainwright Health Centre as injured military members are treated after a fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, outside of Wainwright, Alberta, on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026.
John Ulan/The Canadian Press via AP
"I'm saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base," Defense Minister David McGuinty said.The four who were killed have been identified as:Sergeant Morgan Wong, from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment based at Edmonton, Alberta, serving with 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry; Private Shaun Farrell, from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alberta; Private Aidan Goulding, from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alberta;Private Hayden Lykkemark, from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alberta.The incident occurred at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, located about 112 miles southeast of Edmonton.
Rutland said the cause of the initial grass fire is still under investigation, noting there were "multiple training activities happening throughout the training area at the time."He said the fire crossed "established fire guards" before it was contained with the help of local authorities. He also said reports of explosions were not believed to be the result of the fire reaching oil and gas infrastructure or from "any outside interference." Firefighters faced a volatile situation. Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 100 kilometers (62 miles) an hour. The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets.By 11 p.m., the Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. There was no evacuation order for residents.McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in the investigation and described the situation as "very, very active and delicate.""I cannot recall such an incident in my short time for sure as a minister, but I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory," McGuinty said.The Canadian Armed Forces and federal, provincial and local authorities were coordinating the emergency response, he said. The nearby community of Wainwright was providing hospital and firefighting support.
"Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected," Carney said earlier in a social media post.Smith described the fire as "significant and tragic" and said it was affecting many military personnel.Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is one of Canada's busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.
Paramedics work at the Wainwright Health Centre as injured military members are treated after a fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, outside of Wainwright, Alberta, on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026.
John Ulan/The Canadian Press via AP
Carney said the federal government was working closely with Alberta officials and local authorities. He said he and Smith were in close contact, as were their ministers and officials. Smith thanked first responders and those providing care and support to those affected.Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Carney and the defense minister to offer support to those affected by the fire."Pray for Wainwright, everyone," Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.The fire came days before the province is set to vote on beginning a process that could lead to its seeking independence from Canada.

sources.headline: Carney says cause of fire at Alberta military base still unknown
sources.text: OTTAWA, Oct 19 - Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Monday that the cause of a fire that killed at least four military members and injured dozens of others in Alberta on Saturday is still unknown.Carney said in an address to Parliament that soldiers and reserve members were conducting live-fire exercises at an army base in Wainwright while a fire was burning in the training area.“Driven by ferocious winds, the fire jumped nearly a kilometer in less than a minute to where soldiers were gathered,” Carney said. He added that 50 investigators are currently on the ground, from the army and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, to determine how the disaster happened."This loss touches every corner of the nation," Carney said.Officials said 39 people remain hospitalized, with 19 people in critical condition. The soldiers and reserve members were preparing to deploy to Latvia, where Canadian forces have their largest international military operation.Kent Moore, a professor of atmospheric physics at the University of Toronto, said the embers from grass fires in dry conditions can spread incredibly quickly. He said there didn't appear to be any rain in the area, so it was unlikely the fire was triggered by lightning."The fact that the winds were so strong suggests to me that it wouldn't have taken much to start this fire," he said, speculating that it was likely caused by human error, including sparks from vehicles or live fire, or an errant cigarette from a smoker. REUTERS

sources.headline: Canada reports 'fatalities and injuries' following incident at military base
sources.text:
Published on 18/10/2026 - 9:01 GMT+2•Updated
19/10/2026 - 6:49 GMT+2
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday that four service members were killed and dozens more seriously injured in a fire during a military training at a base in Alberta, calling it one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military on domestic soil.
In a televised address, Carney said the families of those killed had been notified and that the situation was still evolving.
He said the victims were taking part in military training when the fire broke out Saturday. Carney ordered flags to fly at half-staff on federal buildings nationwide in their honour.
Those affected included reservists and soldiers from Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, one of the country’s most storied regiments.
The personnel had travelled from bases across Canada to train at Wainwright. It was not immediately clear how many people were injured, but Carney said the wounded were being treated in Wainwright, Edmonton, Red Deer and Calgary.
Military says cause of incident under investigation
Fire crews rushed to Canadian Forces Base Wainwright late Saturday as fierce winds pushed flames beyond the base and into the surrounding rural area.
The Canadian military said Sunday there were no indications the incident was an act of terrorism, but the cause remains under investigation.
A doctor at a hospital in Edmonton, 180 kilometres (112 miles) northwest of the base, told Canada’s national broadcaster that patients were sent to hospitals across the city because healthcare facilities near the base were “completely overwhelmed.”
Acute Care Alberta said several hospitals across the province had activated a “Code Orange,” an emergency designation used when multiple severely injured patients need coordinated care.
The agency said emergency medical resources were stretched so thin that very few ambulances were available in the Edmonton area. Late Saturday, at least 10 ambulances were parked in and around the Wainwright health centre as paramedics and soldiers rushed about. The town of Wainwright has about 7,000 residents.
The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday’s referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada.
Elections Alberta said the advance polling location at Wainwright Communiplex closed early Saturday, and ballots and election materials were transported securely. It named polling locations in Lloydminster and Vermilion as alternatives.

Fire crews scrambled late Saturday as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area. The Canadian military said Sunday there were no indications that the incident was the result of terrorism, but the cause remained under investigation. Speaking in a televised address, Carney said the families of those killed had been notified and that the situation was still evolving.
Flags would fly at half-staff on federal buildings across the country in honor of those affected by the tragedy, he said. It was not immediately clear exactly how many people had been injured Cathy Keane, a mayoral candidate in Ontario, said her eldest son was among the military personnel critically injured. "As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family," she wrote on Facebook, saying she was traveling to Alberta. A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180 kilometers (112 miles) northwest, told Canada's national broadcaster that patients were taken to hospitals across the city as healthcare facilities around the base became "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people needing care. "This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15- to 25-year disaster." Hospitals declare emergency Acute Care Alberta said several hospitals across the province had activated a "Code Orange," an emergency designation used when multiple severely injured patients require coordinated medical care. The agency said emergency medical resources were stretched so thin that extremely few ambulances were available in the Edmonton area. It urged people to avoid the University of Alberta Hospital emergency department if possible.
Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the town's small hospital was not designed to handle a mass-casualty incident but praised the response of local medical personnel. He said helicopters and planes had been transporting patients to other facilities for treatment. At least 10 ambulances were parked in and around the Wainwright health center late Saturday as paramedics and soldiers rushed about. One patient was seen being loaded into an ambulance. The town of Wainwright, near the base, has about 7,000 residents.
Paramedics load an injured person into an ambulance at the Wainwright Health center after a fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, outside of Wainwright, Alberta Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026.

Military rules out terrorism as cause Defense Minister David McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in investigating the incident and described the situation as "very, very active and delicate." He said authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information. McGuinty said Sunday he was traveling to Edmonton to be briefed on the latest developments. He said the military was working closely with Alberta's government and local authorities. The Canadian Armed Forces said it would not release casualty figures until relatives had been notified. "The full extent of the impact remains under assessment," the military said in a statement late Saturday. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4 p.m. Saturday following reports of a fire in a training area at the base. Firefighters faced a volatile situation. Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 100 kph (62 mph). The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets. By 11 p.m., the Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. There was no evacuation order for residents. McGuinty, speaking to reporters in Ottawa, confirmed the casualties but had no other details to share.
"I cannot recall such an incident in my short time for sure as a minister, but I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory," McGuinty said. "We will have more to say in the coming hours and days," he added. He said Armed Forces members were at the scene and that RCMP were also involved. "This is an active and delicate situation and soon to be an active and delicate investigation." Alberta receives offers of support and assistance Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as "significant and tragic" and said it was affecting many military personnel. CFB Wainwright is one of Canada's busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training. Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Carney and the defense minister to offer support to those affected by the fire. "Pray for Wainwright, everyone," Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders. The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday's referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada. Elections Alberta said two polling locations, in Lloydminster and Vermilion, closed early Saturday and the ballots were transported securely.

sources.headline: Fatal military base fire among Canada's worst peacetime tragedies, PM says
sources.text: A major fire at a Canadian military base has killed at least four people and injured dozens more.The fire erupted late on Saturday, local time, at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta — one of the country's busiest army bases. Fire crews scrambled as winds up to 96 ‌kilometres per hour whipped the flames beyond the base and into the surrounding rural area. Alberta's Premier Danielle Smith said 39 people were hospitalised, at least 19 of which were in a critical condition.Albertans mourn at a church service in Wainwright, a day after the tragedy. (Reuters: Jennifer Gauthier)The fire ignited in an area where personnel were ‌undertaking training drills, Canadian officials said.Major General Wade Rutland described the fire as an "uncommon, rapid" event.“I’ve ⁠certainly never seen anything like it," said Major General Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian ‌Division.Patients were transferred from the base to four hospitals across Alberta, Ms Smith said, confirming some suffered severe burns and could face weeks or months of intensive treatment.An investigation into what caused the blaze is ongoing, but the Canadian military has told local news outlets that as of now there are no indications that it was a result of any terrorist activity.Mark Carney delivered a statement on Parliament Hill. (The Canadian Press via AP: Patrick Doyle)Prime Minister Mark Carney said it was one of the worst tragedies Canadian forces had experienced on domestic soil during peacetime and ordered all flags on federal buildings be flown at half-mast.He said the violent, fast-moving fire swept through the base after breaking out at the base's training area."We will be there for their families for as long as they need," Mr Carney said."We will care for the injured through every step of their recovery, and we will stand by the women and men of the armed forces as they bear the weight of this loss."They will not carry it alone."Hospitals activate 'code orange'Mr Carney said those affected included reservists and soldiers from Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, one of Canada's most storied military regiments.The personnel had come from bases across the country to train at Wainwright.Cathy Keane, a mayoral candidate in Ontario, said her eldest son was among the military personnel critically injured."As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family," she wrote on Facebook, saying she was travelling to Alberta.Acute Care Alberta said several hospitals across the province had activated a "code orange", an emergency designation used when multiple severely injured patients require coordinated medical care.Strong winds pushed flames beyond the base and into the surrounding rural area. (Reuters: Jennifer Gauthier)The agency said emergency medical resources were stretched so thin that extremely few ambulances were available in the Edmonton area.It urged people to avoid the University of Alberta Hospital emergency department if possible.Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the town's small hospital was not designed to handle a mass-casualty incident but praised the response of local medical personnel.Paramedics load an injured person into an ambulance at the Wainwright Health Center after a fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright. (The Canadian Press via AP: John Ulan)He said helicopters and planes transported patients to other facilities for treatment.At least 10 ambulances were parked in and around the Wainwright health centre late on Saturday as paramedics and soldiers rushed about.The town of Wainwright, near the base, has about 7,000 residents.ABC/AP
